name: Aisi
confidence_why: Word-final stress for Aisi rests on Daniels (2010), who from his own 2006 field data states that stress is 'almost always word-final' in the Sogeram daughter languages, Aisi among them; no source describes Aisi stress directly (Daniels's 2015 Aisi grammar sketch, his 2016 article and his 2020 book are silent, the last calling for further research on Sogeram stress), and nothing contradicts it.
catalog_citation: Daniels, Don R. 2010. A preliminary phonological history of the Sogeram languages of Papua New Guinea. Oceanic Linguistics 49(1): 163-193. doi:10.1353/ol.0.0068 (Project MUSE publisher PDF, obtained through the library by hand 2026-09-18).
catalog_locator: p. 168, §2 'Proto-Sogeram', the sentence directly after the PSOG phoneme inventory (1); supporting mentions p. 175 §4.1.2 'Vowel centering' and p. 177 §4.3.1; Aisi section §5.2 'Aisi innovations' pp. 181-182 has no stress statement. Aisi named as one of the daughter languages treated: p. 164 'Aisi (Musak)', §5.2 pp. 181-182.
catalog_quote: Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG. [p. 168] ... 4.1.2 Vowel centering (V-R > ɨ / C__C.’σopen). Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change. [p. 175] ... While this innovation is not a bizarre phonetic development, the fact that these languages probably had word-final stress makes it a little peculiar. [p. 177]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 32 pp., Project MUSE text). All three quoted sentences are verbatim in the : p. 168 (the text layerbetween the '168 OCEANIC LINGUISTICS' running head and the next form feed), directly after PSOG inventory (1) in §2: 'Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG.' p. 175 §4.1.2 (line 643-644): 'Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change.' p. 177 §4.3.1 (lines 705-706, under the 'PHONOLOGICAL HISTORY.. 177' head): 'While this innovation is not a bizarre phonetic development, the fact that these lan-guages probably had…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for Aisi, so there is nothing to agree or disagree with; this is the first statement found. It is a family-wide claim ('the daughter languages'), not a description of Aisi itself, so it supports fixed: final syllable for Aisi only by inclusion. Confidence for Aisi specifically is medium-low.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A family-level generalization: stress falls on the last syllable of the word in (almost) all Sogeram daughter languages, Aisi among them (Aisi is one of the eight languages treated, §5.2 pp. 181-182), and Daniels reconstructs word-final stress for Proto-Sogeram. No Aisi-specific stress statement and no examples with stress marked; §5.2 'Aisi innovations' (pp. 181-182) says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost always' — the author hedges that word-final stress is not exceptionless across the daughter languages, but names no exceptions and no language-specific pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Aisi is the speakers' own name (their word for 'why'); Z'graggen's name 'Musak' (the Glottolog name behind musa1266) is a village name (Daniels 2010 p. 164: 'Aisi (Musak)'; Daniels 2020 pp. 4-5). Daniels 2015 called the language 'Mabɨŋ' (Daniels 2020 p. 5 n. 1). Aisi (c. 350 speakers, four villages southeast of Apalɨ between the Sogeram and Ramu rivers, 2010 pp. 181-182) forms the 'Aisian' unit with Magɨ, a closely related but not mutually intelligible language first distinguished by Daniels (2020 p. 4); Daniels 2010 predates that split and its 'Aisi' data are the Musak-village variety. Neither work describes a dialect of Aisi.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction. Daniels 2010 (p. 168) states that stress is 'almost always word-final in the daughter languages' of Proto-Sogeram, which includes Aisi; Daniels 2020 makes no statement about Aisi, confirms word-final stress only for Manat (p. 65) and says that 'further research into the stress systems of the Sogeram languages' is needed (p. 60). The 2020 hedge does not retract the 2010 generalization, but it shows the family-level claim was never backed by a per-language description, so fixed: final syllable for Aisi rests on inclusion in a family-wide 'almost always', not on an Aisi-specific analysis.

sources.citation: Daniels, Don Roger. 2015. A Reconstruction of Proto-Sogeram: Phonology, Lexicon, and Morphosyntax. sources.note: Nothing for Aisi. Sec. 4.2 (pp. 771-776) covers consonant/vowel inventories, /b d g/ lenition to [β ɾ ɣ] non-initially, status of /r/, diphthongs /ai/ and /ou/~/au/, glide vs vowel syllabification, minimal pairs for /ɨ/, and morphophonemics (ɨ-epenthesis, rounding, nasal assimilation); no word on stress, accent, tone or syllable weight. sources.note: No stress statement. p. 74 sec. 2.22.8 item 2, for the whole Adelbert Range Phylum (which includes Musak): 'None of the languages appears to be tonal.'
